Inside the E2SFCA calculation

Source: vignettes/e2sfca-steps.Rmd
e2sfca-steps.Rmd

The enhanced two-step floating catchment area (E2SFCA) index gives each place the GP supply per resident within reach, with weights that fall with travel time. This guide rebuilds the index of Getting started one step at a time from the building blocks of spax, and compares the result with spax(). By the end you can say where each cell’s number comes from, swap one set of weights to get another index, and see why the calculation has to cover the whole study area. The inputs are the mainland grids of The Cornwall GP example data. The spax() interface and the allocation model are experimental and may change in later versions.

library(spax)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)

The formula

A floating catchment area (FCA) index has two steps. First each facility gathers the demand around it and divides its supply by that demand. Then each place adds up the ratios of the facilities it can reach. Here demand is the residents of a grid cell and supply is a practice’s GP full-time equivalents (FTE).

Let demand at cell ii be DiD_i and supply at practice jj be SjS_j. The weights GijG_{ij} decide how much of cell ii’s demand practice jj gathers, and the weights HijH_{ij} how much of practice jj’s ratio cell ii receives. Then

Lj=∑iDiGij,Rj=Sj/Lj,Ai=∑jHijRj. L_j=\sum_i D_iG_{ij},\qquad R_j=S_j/L_j,\qquad A_i=\sum_j H_{ij}R_j.

LjL_j is the demand practice jj gathers, RjR_j its supply-to-demand ratio and AiA_i the index at cell ii. E2SFCA uses the same decay weights WijW_{ij}, which fall with the travel time from cell ii to practice jj (step 1), for both: G=H=WG = H = W.

The inputs

The setup code shared by every grid guide, explained in The Cornwall GP example data, reads the population grid, the mainland practices and one layer of travel minutes per practice. The supply is also kept as a vector named by practice code, and a small helper maps a layer around Truro so that single cells stay visible.

gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
travel_grid <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")[[gp$practice]]
# Keep cells with a travel time to every mainland practice
pop <- trim(mask(pop, sum(travel_grid)))
travel_grid <- crop(travel_grid, pop)
grid_data <- prep_data(pop, gp, travel_grid, id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")

# GP FTE named by practice code
supply <- setNames(gp$gp_fte_extg, gp$practice)

# Map helper: a layer within the Truro display window, with practices
truro_window <- ext(-5.30, -4.80, 50.12, 50.42)
practices <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  vect()
coast <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_union() |>
  vect()
show <- function(layer, title) {
  plot(
    crop(layer, truro_window),
    axes = FALSE,
    main = title,
    col = hcl.colors(50, "viridis")
  )
  lines(crop(coast, truro_window), lwd = 0.6)
  points(crop(practices, truro_window), pch = 3, col = "red")
}

The calculation covers all of mainland Cornwall. Only the maps zoom in.

Step 1: decay weights

With Gaussian decay, Wij=exp⁡(−dij2/(2σ2))W_{ij}=\exp\!\left(-d_{ij}^2/(2\sigma^2)\right), where dijd_{ij} is the travel time and σ is the travel scale. We use σ = 10 minutes, a choice for this guide. calc_decay() works on plain numbers and on rasters alike.

# The weight left after a few travel times
minutes <- c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30)
weight_left <- calc_decay(minutes, method = "gaussian", sigma = 10)
round(setNames(weight_left, minutes), 3)
    0     5    10    15    20    30 
1.000 0.882 0.607 0.325 0.135 0.011 
# The same decay applied to every travel layer
weights <- calc_decay(travel_grid, method = "gaussian", sigma = 10)
show(
  weights[["L82001"]],
  "Step 1: weight of one Truro practice (L82001), 0 to 1"
)

A practice 10 minutes away keeps 61% of the weight it would have next door, and one 30 minutes away about 1%. Each practice has one weight layer. The map shows the layer for L82001, a practice in central Truro: it is the red cross at the center of the bright area (the other crosses are other practices). The weight is close to 1 near it and fades with travel time. The shape follows the travel-time surface rather than straight-line distance, and the gaps are estuaries.

Step 2 (optional): normalize the demand-side weights

The weights of all practices at one cell can add up to more than 1. Where many practices are close, each of them counts the same resident. calc_normalize() can rescale them: "standard" (its default) divides each cell’s weights by their sum, and "semi" does so only where the sum exceeds 1. "identity", the default of spec_e2sfca(), leaves them as they are. The table gives cell quantiles of the summed weights, before and after.

# Sum of all practices' weights at each cell
cell_sum <- function(layers) values(sum(layers), mat = FALSE)
probs <- c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)

standard <- calc_normalize(weights, method = "standard")
semi <- calc_normalize(weights, method = "semi")

round(
  rbind(
    identity = quantile(cell_sum(weights), probs, na.rm = TRUE),
    standard = quantile(cell_sum(standard), probs, na.rm = TRUE),
    semi = quantile(cell_sum(semi), probs, na.rm = TRUE)
  ),
  2
)
           5%  50%  95%
identity 1.23 3.96 9.06
standard 1.00 1.00 1.00
semi     1.00 1.00 1.00

At the median cell the weights sum to 3.96, and even at the 5th percentile they sum to 1.23. So "standard" and "semi" give almost the same result here, and both differ from "identity". The choice changes the demand each practice gathers and so the index: normalization is part of the model you choose. spec_e2sfca(normalize = ) applies it to the demand side only. We keep "identity", the default, so G=H=WG = H = W.

Step 3: gather demand to practices

gather_weighted() sums demand times weight over all cells for each practice: Lj=∑iDiWijL_j=\sum_i D_iW_{ij}. With simplify = TRUE it returns a vector named by the weight layers.

gathered <- gather_weighted(
  values = pop,
  weights = weights,
  simplify = TRUE  # one named value per practice
)
round(head(gathered))
L82001 L82003 L82004 L82006 L82007 L82008 
 95347  22747  42324  91637  21265  16840

The names are the practice codes, which step 4 uses to line up the supply. Each value is the weighted number of residents a practice gathers. A resident within reach of several practices counts toward each of them, so these values, over all 54 practices, add up to 5.9 times the mainland’s residents.

Step 4: supply-to-demand ratios

Each practice’s ratio is its supply over the demand it gathered, Rj=Sj/LjR_j=S_j/L_j. Index the supply by the names of gathered, not by position. The table shows six practices near Truro.

ratio <- supply[names(gathered)] / gathered

# Supply, gathered demand and ratio for six practices near Truro
near_truro <- c("L82001", "L82028", "L82015", "L82061", "L82045", "L82048")
data.frame(practice = near_truro) |>
  left_join(select(gp, practice, name), by = "practice") |>
  mutate(
    gp_fte = round(supply[practice], 1),
    weighted_residents = round(gathered[practice]),
    fte_per_1000 = round(1000 * ratio[practice], 2)
  )
  practice                          name gp_fte weighted_residents fte_per_1000
1   L82001       LANDER MEDICAL PRACTICE   10.3              95347         0.11
2   L82028 THREE SPIRES MEDICAL PRACTICE   10.3              95347         0.11
3   L82015      CHACEWATER HEALTH CENTRE    3.7             105955         0.04
4   L82061          CARNON DOWNS SURGERY    5.3             100581         0.05
5   L82045                PROBUS SURGERY    6.6              71415         0.09
6   L82048            ROSELAND SURGERIES    3.3              42552         0.08

The ratios look small because, with identity weights, each resident is counted by several practices. Step 5 adds them back up. The two central Truro practices share one site, so they gather the same demand. With a decay that reaches zero, such as a fixed catchment, a practice can gather no demand. spax gives it a ratio of zero, but the division above gives Inf, so set those ratios to 0 when you calculate by hand.

Step 5: spread the ratios back to cells

spread_weighted() multiplies each practice’s ratio by its weight layer and sums over practices: Ai=∑jWijRjA_i=\sum_j W_{ij}R_j. It matches values to layers by position, so pass the ratios in layer order.

# Ratios in layer order, without names: matching is by position
access <- spread_weighted(
  values = unname(ratio[names(weights)]),
  weights = weights
)
show(1000 * access, "Step 5: E2SFCA, GP FTE per 1,000 residents")

The index is highest in a band west and south-west of Truro and falls towards the east of the window, where fewer practices are close. A cell’s index is a sum of contributions from every practice. For the cell that contains the central Truro practice, the largest contributions are, in GP FTE per 1,000 residents:

# The grid cell that contains practice L82001
site <- geom(practices[practices$practice == "L82001", ])
cell <- cellFromXY(pop, site[, c("x", "y"), drop = FALSE])

# Each practice's contribution: its weight at the cell times its ratio
weights_at_cell <- unlist(extract(weights, cell))
contributions <- sort(
  1000 * weights_at_cell * ratio[names(weights_at_cell)],
  decreasing = TRUE
)

round(
  c(
    head(contributions, 5),
    all_others = sum(contributions[-(1:5)]),
    total = sum(contributions)
  ),
  3
)
    L82028     L82001     L82045     L82006     L82061 all_others      total 
     0.108      0.107      0.067      0.048      0.047      0.417      0.794

The two practices at the central Truro site contribute most. The other 49 practices beyond the top five still add 53% of the cell’s index.

The same index from spax()

The surface built by hand, access, should match the index from spax(), the one-call function spax_e2sfca() and the more general compute_access(). compute_access() takes the two weight sets GG and HH of the formula as demand_weights and access_weights, so it can build any index of this form. Each comparison below prints TRUE when the two surfaces agree, cell by cell and in which cells are empty.

# The index from a specification
by_spec <- spax(grid_data, spec_e2sfca(decay = decay_gaussian(sigma = 10)))

# The one-call function
one_call <- spax_e2sfca(
  demand = pop,
  supply = gp,
  distance = travel_grid,
  decay_params = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 10),
  id_col = "practice",
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg"
)

# The general function, with the decay weights on both sides
general <- compute_access(
  demand = pop,
  supply = supply,
  demand_weights = weights,
  access_weights = weights
)

# Compare a surface with the one built by hand
same_as_by_hand <- function(surface) {
  all.equal(values(surface, mat = FALSE), values(access, mat = FALSE))
}
c(
  spax = same_as_by_hand(by_spec$accessibility),
  spax_e2sfca = same_as_by_hand(one_call$accessibility),
  compute_access = same_as_by_hand(general)
)
          spax    spax_e2sfca compute_access 
          TRUE           TRUE           TRUE

all.equal() allows for rounding error in the last digits, and every route agrees. Each computes the same three quantities: gathered demand, ratios and the weighted sum of ratios.

Change the access-side weights: M2SFCA

The modified 2SFCA (M2SFCA) keeps WW on the demand side but uses W2W^2 on the access side, so G=WG = W and H=W2H = W^2. W2W^2 is below WW except at zero travel time, and far below it for distant practices, so M2SFCA discounts cells whose practices are far away. Swap the access-side weights for their squares and compute_access() gives M2SFCA.

m2sfca <- spax(grid_data, spec_m2sfca(decay = decay_gaussian(sigma = 10)))

# M2SFCA from the blocks: squared weights on the access side only
m2sfca_by_blocks <- compute_access(
  demand = pop,
  supply = supply,
  demand_weights = weights,
  access_weights = weights^2
)
all.equal(
  values(m2sfca_by_blocks, mat = FALSE),
  values(m2sfca$accessibility, mat = FALSE)
)
[1] TRUE

The two agree: M2SFCA differs from E2SFCA only in the weights of step 5.

Other indices from the same blocks

The three-step FCA (3SFCA) and Huff-2SFCA share each cell’s demand among its practices before the two steps. calc_choice() turns the decay weights into selection weights: each practice’s share of the cell’s weights, which add up to 1 at every cell. With an attractiveness, here GP FTE, each weight is first multiplied by it, as in the Huff model. Both indices then use the decay weight times the selection weight in both steps, and compute_access() does the rest.

# 3SFCA: each cell's weights divided by their sum
selection <- calc_choice(weights)
range(values(sum(selection), mat = FALSE), na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 1 1
sfca3_weights <- weights * selection
sfca3_by_blocks <- compute_access(pop, supply, sfca3_weights, sfca3_weights)

# Huff-2SFCA: the same, with each weight times the practice's GP FTE
huff_selection <- calc_choice(weights, attractiveness = supply)
huff_weights <- weights * huff_selection
huff_by_blocks <- compute_access(pop, supply, huff_weights, huff_weights)

# The same indices from spax()
sfca3 <- spax(grid_data, spec_3sfca(decay = decay_gaussian(sigma = 10)))
huff2sfca <- spax(grid_data, spec_huff2sfca(decay = decay_gaussian(sigma = 10)))
c(
  `3SFCA` = all.equal(
    values(sfca3_by_blocks, mat = FALSE),
    values(sfca3$accessibility, mat = FALSE)
  ),
  `Huff-2SFCA` = all.equal(
    values(huff_by_blocks, mat = FALSE),
    values(huff2sfca$accessibility, mat = FALSE)
  )
)
     3SFCA Huff-2SFCA 
      TRUE       TRUE

The selection weights add up to 1 at every cell, as the range shows, and both rebuilds agree with spax(). The same blocks build an index of your own: any two weight stacks on the grid of the demand can go into compute_access(). Which FCA index? maps these indices side by side.

Why the calculation covers the whole mainland

Cropping the inputs to the Truro window before calculating would be quicker. But every practice, including those outside the window, would then gather only the demand inside it. The output gives cell quantiles of the percentage difference between the cropped and the full calculation, for cells in the window.

# Calculate on the Truro window only
truro_data <- prep_data(
  crop(pop, truro_window),
  gp,
  crop(travel_grid, truro_window),
  id_col = "practice",
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg"
)
cropped <- spax(truro_data, spec_e2sfca(decay = decay_gaussian(sigma = 10)))

# Compare with the full calculation over the same cells
in_window <- values(crop(by_spec$accessibility, truro_window), mat = FALSE)
relative <- values(cropped$accessibility, mat = FALSE) / in_window - 1
round(quantile(100 * relative, c(0, 0.5, 1), na.rm = TRUE), 1)
    0%    50%   100% 
  15.5   54.5 4980.0

Every cell’s index rises: by 15.5% at the least affected cell and 54.5% at the median. The worst cell, on the window’s edge, rises to about 51 times its full value. It picks up practices outside the window, whose small remaining demand gives them very high ratios. Calculate on the full study area and crop only for display.
